client: I've been avoiding my friends lately. Every time I go out with them and they're laughing and having fun, I just feel this heavy guilt, like I shouldn't be enjoying myself when my brother can't. It's been six months but the pain feels just as fresh, and I'm not sure talking about it will change that.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying this deep sense of guilt with you, and it’s making it hard to connect with others or allow yourself moments of joy. Would it feel okay to explore what thoughts come up when you're with your friends and that guilt arises?

client: I guess when I'm with them, I start thinking, "Why should I be allowed to laugh and have fun when my brother can't?" It feels unfair, like I'm betraying him by moving on. I don’t know if exploring it will help—it feels like this guilt is just part of who I am now.
therapist: I hear how deeply this belief sits with you—that allowing yourself joy somehow dishonors your brother's memory. That sense of unfairness sounds like it's become woven into how you see yourself now. Could we gently examine together whether your brother would have wanted this ongoing guilt for you?

client: That question actually makes me tear up a little. He was always telling me not to take life so seriously, to enjoy the little things... But that almost makes it worse, like I'm failing him by not living the way he'd want me to. The guilt gets even heavier when I think about that.
therapist: It sounds like this realization is bringing up both sadness and a complicated layer of guilt—almost like you're caught between his wishes and your own pain. When you notice that heavier guilt coming up, what happens if you pause and ask yourself: "What would my brother say to me right now?"

client: I think he’d probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself and to go enjoy life... but that feels easier said than done. Even if I know that’s what he’d say, it doesn’t take away the guilt. It’s like my brain knows one thing, but my heart feels something completely different.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real tug-of-war happening between what you know logically and what you feel emotionally, and that disconnect must be so hard to sit with. When you notice that gap between your thoughts and feelings, what’s it like to try and hold space for both, rather than letting one override the other?

client: I don't know if I can do that. When I try to acknowledge both, it just makes me feel more torn apart. The logical part seems so weak compared to the guilt—like it's getting drowned out. Maybe I don't deserve to feel better yet.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming that clash feels—like the guilt is this tidal wave, and the logical part can barely keep its head above water. That sense of not deserving relief yet sounds like it’s carrying a lot of weight for you. Would it be okay to explore what "deserving" to feel better might look like for you?

client: I don't even know what "deserving" would mean—it's not about earning anything. It just feels like the pain and guilt are what connect me to him now. If I let that go, what's left? That scares me almost more than the guilt does.
therapist: It sounds like this guilt has become a way to hold onto your brother, and the thought of letting it go feels like losing that connection—which must be so frightening. What if we gently explore together what other ways might exist to feel close to him, without carrying the weight of guilt?

client: I never thought about it that way—that the guilt might be my way of staying connected. But now that you say it... I do worry that if I stop feeling guilty, I'll forget him somehow. Even though that probably sounds irrational. It's just that the pain feels like proof of how much he mattered to me.
therapist: It sounds like this guilt has become tangled up with your love and memories of him, as if letting go of the pain might somehow diminish his importance. That fear of forgetting him—even if it feels irrational—makes so much sense when you’re grieving. What would it feel like to explore ways to honor his memory that don’t depend on carrying this pain?

client: I guess I’ve never really thought about that—ways to honor him without the pain. It feels scary, like if I try to find joy or connection in other ways, I’ll lose something important. But at the same time, I’m so exhausted from carrying this guilt all the time. I just don’t know if I’m ready to let go of it yet.
therapist: It sounds like you're standing at this crossroads—exhausted by the weight of the guilt, but also scared of what might happen if you loosen your grip on it. That fear of losing something important is completely understandable. Could we explore together what small steps might feel manageable to start honoring your brother in a way that feels more gentle on your heart?

client: I guess small steps could feel less overwhelming... but I’m not sure where to start. Even thinking about honoring him in a different way makes me feel guilty, like I’m trying to "fix" something that shouldn’t be fixed. How do I know if I’m ready for that?
therapist: It sounds like even the idea of taking small steps brings up uncertainty and a bit of guilt, as if changing how you honor him might feel like you’re dismissing his memory—which of course isn’t the case at all. That hesitation makes so much sense when you’re navigating such deep emotions. What if we start by simply reflecting on what feels meaningful to you about your brother, without any pressure to "fix" or change anything yet?

client: Reflecting on what feels meaningful about him... I guess what comes to mind is how much he loved music and how he always wanted me to enjoy life more. But even thinking about that makes me feel sad and guilty—like I’m not living up to what he’d want for me. I don’t know if focusing on those memories will help or just make me feel worse.
therapist: It sounds like these meaningful memories are bringing up both love and sadness—and that the guilt is still there, whispering that you're not living up to his hopes for you. That mix of emotions must feel so heavy. What would it feel like to hold those memories gently, without judging yourself for how they make you feel right now?
